title: FRANCHISE OR EMPIRE?
subtitle: The structural resonances — and the crucial difference — between corporate franchising and imperial patron-client systems.
source: Doyle, M. (1986). Empires; Gallagher, J. & Robinson, R. (1953). The Imperialism of Free Trade.

sourceElements.label: Franchisee Invests Own Capital
sourceElements.description: Local operator bears financial risk; parent extracts royalties.

sourceElements.label: Standardized Product Rules
sourceElements.description: Brand dictates quality, pricing, and operational norms.

sourceElements.label: Franchisor Owns the Brand
sourceElements.description: Intellectual property and ultimate identity stay at the top.

sourceElements.label: Franchisee Keeps Some Margin
sourceElements.description: Local operator retains a negotiated share of revenue.

sourceElements.label: Brand-Level Risk Pooling
sourceElements.description: One operator's failure can damage all franchisees' reputations.

targetElements.label: Client Provides Soldiers/Resources
targetElements.description: Periphery contributes manpower and tribute to the imperial center.

targetElements.label: Imperial Norms Enforced
targetElements.description: Hegemon dictates legal, monetary, and military standards.

targetElements.label: Hegemon Controls Strategy
targetElements.description: Core power retains monopoly on grand-strategic decisions.

targetElements.label: Client Retains Domestic Governance
targetElements.description: Local rulers manage internal affairs within hegemon-set limits.

targetElements.label: Collective Security Umbrella
targetElements.description: Alliance credibility depends on perceived willingness to defend any member.

breakNote: The analogy breaks at voluntariness and exit. Franchise contracts are entered voluntarily, precisely specified, and terminable by either party with legal recourse. Imperial patron-client relationships are typically not: client states rarely negotiate from a position of symmetry, and exit from the imperial orbit — defection, non-alignment, regime change — is met with coercion or military intervention, not contract litigation. The franchise metaphor illuminates the extraction logic and norm-setting architecture; it obscures the coercive foundation that makes the system sticky.
